origin_region: Fujian · Wuyi Mountains · Tongmu (home of Lapsang Souchong); smoked teas are also made in Hunan, Yunnan and by Western blenders
cultivar: Wuyi Caicha (local small-leaf bushes) for Tongmu Lapsang; various for other smoked teas
processing: Tea is dried, and sometimes withered, over smouldering pine in a smokehouse: in the Tongmu tradition the leaf is withered on racks above a pine fire, rolled, oxidised, pan-fired and then finished over pine smoke, so the smoke is part of the making. Many modern 'smoked' teas are smoked after processing, and cheap ones are made with liquid smoke flavouring.
harvest_season: Spring, April to May, for the Wuyi originals; Western smoked blends are made year-round from stock tea.
appearance_dry: Dark, glossy, slightly oily black leaf with a strong pine-and-tar smell; heavily smoked export grades are blacker and more pungent than lightly smoked Tongmu lots.
appearance_wet: Dark copper leaf, the smoke softer and sweeter once wet.
taste_profile: Pine smoke, tar and a bacon-like savouriness over a sweet, malty black tea with dried longan and a cooling finish; lightly smoked originals are balanced and fruity, heavy export styles are campfire first and tea second.

brewing.notes: Gongfu with short steeps shows the fruit behind the smoke; Western style, 3 g per 250 ml for 3 minutes. Heavily smoked teas take milk and are the classic match for smoked fish, cheese and a full breakfast. The smoke mellows noticeably after a year or two in a sealed tin.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest for Tongmu originals, with the smoke level the main variable: lightly smoked traditional lots, heavily smoked export grades (sometimes called Tarry Souchong), and, most Tongmu production today, unsmoked 'Zheng Shan Xiao Zhong', which is a completely different, honeyed tea under the same name. Western blends such as Russian Caravan use a proportion of smoked leaf and are sold year-round. Smoked teas keep well for several years and soften with age; a tin of heavy Lapsang is often better in its second year.
description:
Smoked tea is the tea that smells of a campfire, and almost all of it descends from one place: Tongmu village in the Wuyi Mountains of Fujian, where Lapsang Souchong was first dried over pine fires, probably as a way to finish tea fast in the damp mountain spring. It became a British favourite in the nineteenth century, and heavy, tarry export grades were made to suit that taste.

The method is the whole style. In Tongmu the leaf is withered on bamboo racks in a smokehouse above a slow pine fire, rolled and oxidised, then dried again over pine smoke, so the smoke is woven in at two stages and the result is layered, with dried longan and malt underneath. Elsewhere, and for the export market, finished tea is simply smoked hard afterwards, which gives the bonfire effect, and the cheapest versions use smoke flavouring and taste of it.

A good smoked tea is a surprise: brewed short and hot, the smoke sits on top of a sweet, fruity black tea rather than replacing it, and the cup is savoury, cooling and long. The common mistake is stewing it, which turns pine into ashtray. It takes milk if the smoke is heavy, and it is the best tea in the world for smoked salmon, bacon and strong cheese.

When buying, the first question is smoke level, the second is whether it was smoked in the making or afterwards, and the third is to note that most Tongmu tea now sold as Zheng Shan Xiao Zhong is unsmoked. Smoked teas keep for years and soften, so an older tin is no problem.

If you like the idea but find Lapsang too much, Russian Caravan dilutes it with Keemun and oolong, and a lightly smoked Tongmu lot is the refined end of the style.
